**To:** Infrastructure Working Group
**From:** Platform Engineering
**Date:** 2025-06-12
**Subject:** Acquiring new local AI hardware versus improving utilisation of existing capacity

The question in front of us is deceptively simple: should we spend capital on additional local AI hardware, or should we work harder to get more out of the fleet we already own? I have been thinking about this in terms of five things that rarely appear on the same page of a spec sheet but all matter here: cost, latency, reliability, opportunity cost, and reversibility. My recommendation, stated up front, is that we invest in utilisation first and defer any hardware purchase until we have measured what our current machines are actually doing under load.

Start with cost, because it is the factor that gets discussed most and understood least. The sticker price of a new GPU node is only the beginning. There is rack space, power draw, cooling, networking, spares, and the quiet ongoing tax of firmware updates and driver maintenance that a small team pays in attention rather than dollars. Our current machines were purchased under different constraints and are not fully saturated; adding capacity before we understand why the existing capacity is idle risks buying a solution to a problem we do not actually have. The utilisation path, by contrast, is cheap in cash and expensive in engineering time, which is a trade we are better positioned to make.

Latency is where the analysis gets interesting. If our queues are long because demand genuinely exceeds supply, then more hardware buys latency improvements that compound: shorter queue times, faster iteration for researchers, snappier user experiences. But if the queues are long because of scheduling inefficiency, checkpoint thrash, or jobs that hold GPUs while idle, then latency is a symptom of waste rather than scarcity, and no amount of new silicon will fix the underlying rhythm of the system. Before we buy, we need to know which problem we have, and the honest answer today is that we do not know with precision.

Reliability cuts both ways. New hardware is, statistically, less likely to fail in its first year, and a failed node in a small fleet is not a nuisance but an event that concentrates risk. A single machine going down can take a critical training run or an inference service with it. On the other hand, the reliability of a system we do not fully understand is illusory; if we cannot predict when a machine will be contended, we cannot promise anyone a service level. Improving utilisation means instrumenting our fleet, and instrumentation is itself a reliability investment because it tells us what is about to break before it breaks.

Opportunity cost is the factor I would ask the group to weigh most heavily. Every engineer-week spent on procurement, racking, and tuning new hardware is an engineer-week not spent on the product work that actually pays the bills. If the utilisation work — better scheduling, right-sizing jobs, batching, model quantization where quality permits — can recover even a modest fraction of our current idle capacity, the return on that effort likely exceeds the marginal value of another node. And the capital we would spend on hardware is capital we cannot spend on anything else; that is the definition of opportunity cost, and it deserves a place at the table next to the purchase order.

Reversibility is my final consideration, and it is the one that most clearly separates the two options. A utilisation improvement is almost perfectly reversible: if a scheduling change turns out to hurt, we roll it back. A hardware purchase is a one-way door. We can resell a node, but we will never recover the time it took to choose, order, receive, and deploy it, and resale values for GPU hardware are notoriously unforgiving. When the two options are otherwise comparable, the more reversible one deserves the decision.

I want to be candid about the uncertainty. Our monitoring is good at telling us what happened and weak at telling us what would have happened with more capacity, so the counterfactual — what we would gain from new hardware — is genuinely hard to estimate. There is a real chance that utilisation work recovers only a few percent and that the honest answer turns out to be "buy the node." I would not want us to mistake a recommendation for a certainty.

Accordingly, I recommend the following course of action, framed as a commitment rather than a wish. We should spend the next six weeks on a focused utilisation effort: instrument job-level GPU utilization, identify and eliminate idle-holding patterns, and right-size our queue. In parallel, we should prepare but not execute a hardware purchase plan, so that if the data at the end of the period shows genuine scarcity, we can move quickly. This path is cheap, mostly reversible, and — most importantly — it buys us the information that the decision actually depends on.

I am happy to discuss this at Thursday's meeting.

**To:** Platform Engineering
**From:** [Name]
**Date:** [Date]
**Subject:** Local AI hardware expansion vs. utilisation improvement

We need to decide whether to spend capital on additional local inference and training hardware or to invest engineering effort in getting more out of what we already own. My recommendation, stated up front: improve utilisation first, and treat any hardware purchase as a gated follow-on decision with explicit tripwires. The reasoning below is worth spelling out because the two options are not symmetric in cost, latency behaviour, reliability, or reversibility.

Start with cost, because it is the most obvious and the least informative. A new node is not its sticker price. Once you add power, cooling, rack space, a faster interconnect if the node must talk to existing ones, additional storage, a maintenance contract, and the probability that a component fails outside warranty, the true three-year cost of ownership is commonly 1.5 to 2 times the acquisition price. Depreciation schedules make this look tidy on a spreadsheet and hide it in reality. Utilisation work, by contrast, is almost entirely operating expense: a few weeks of a couple of engineers' time. That is a small, flexible, and largely recoverable investment. If we are currently running our fleet at low average utilisation, the cheapest inference is the one we have already paid for.

Latency deserves more care than it usually gets, because the intuition that "more hardware means lower latency" is only true under specific conditions. Latency in a saturated queue degrades nonlinearly; a cluster running at 40 percent utilisation will not get meaningfully faster by adding capacity, because requests are not waiting on compute. If our measured p95 latencies are within budget and the queue is not backing up, additional hardware buys us nothing on this axis. If, on the other hand, we are routinely near saturation and p95 is spiking, then latency is a symptom of a capacity ceiling and no amount of scheduling cleverness will fix it. This is the single most important empirical question in the decision, and it is answerable with two weeks of instrumentation before we commit a dollar.

Reliability cuts in a less obvious direction. Adding hardware adds failure surface: more drives, more NICs, more firmware to keep current, more nodes whose drift we must monitor. A small cluster also gives us no meaningful redundancy, so a single node failure can take a quarter of our capacity offline. Improving utilisation, if done by consolidating workloads onto fewer healthy nodes, can actually worsen this exposure, which is why I am not proposing aggressive consolidation. The honest framing is that neither option is a reliability programme; both need a separate conversation about redundancy and failure domains.

Opportunity cost is where I expect the strongest disagreement, so I want to be direct. Engineering attention is finite, and every week spent on capacity planning, benchmarking, and vendor evaluation is a week not spent on the product work that actually moves the business. Capital is also finite, and money tied up in depreciating assets is money we cannot spend on the things that compound: people, tooling, and the software that runs on top of the hardware. There is a real sense in which buying hardware now forecloses options we have not yet imagined.

Reversibility is the tiebreaker. A scheduling change, a batching improvement, a model quantisation, a right-sizing of instance types — all of these are cheap to try and cheap to undo. We can measure, revert, and try again within days. Hardware is close to the opposite: a sunk, illiquid asset with a thin resale market and a depreciation curve that punishes early disposal. Once the box is in the rack, the decision is effectively permanent for its useful life. When options are asymmetric in this way, the correct move is to spend the cheap, reversible currency first and preserve the expensive, irreversible one.

So: no purchase this quarter. Instead, instrument utilisation and queue depth for two weeks, apply the obvious software levers — dynamic batching, request coalescing, model right-sizing, scheduling against idle capacity — and re-evaluate. I will buy hardware only if we are demonstrably latency-bound and the software levers have been exhausted. I hold this view with reasonable but not complete confidence. If our growth forecast is materially steeper than I believe, or if the instrumentation reveals we are already at the ceiling, I would expect this recommendation to be wrong, and I would want to revisit it quickly rather than defend it.
